title: Mellemrum
shortIntro: Optimizing code and design for a local culture and event platform.
about:
Mellemrum was a case given to us about a fictional site that mimicked a quickly made protoype with inconsistent user experience and a hastily made code that's hard to continue to develop. We were to clean up the code so it was easier to further develop and tighten the user flow and interactions.

Mellemrum itself was given this description: A local culture and event platform where users can find and sign up for talks, workshops, and other events. The primary target audience are people interested in local culture and events with the secondary being the people hosting these events.

solution.title: Initial review
solution.description:
I went over the code and the design to identify inconsistencies and areas that needed improvement.

I sorted the problems into categories and planned how to fix each. I cut out some of them since the website is a prototype so I couldn't set up something like a log in or email confirmation. I prioritized the issues based on how big of an obstacle they would be for the user.

solution.title: The optimization
solution.description:
I started with cleaning up the code, editing classnames and separating everything into smaller, more manageable files. I aimed for a CSS file with around 100 lines at max and classnames connected to the page they belonged to. For an example, if an eyebrow was related to the about page then the name would be aboutEyebrow.

I sorted all the pages and components into folders with the JSX file and a module CSS file.

Then it was time to edit the page itself. I fixed spacing issues, font sizes, and added a phone number to the sign up sheet but focused on what the user would need from the website.I started first by considering what the primary focus group would need. I added bit more information about the events, the ability to contact the hosts, and a contact page to Mellemrum. They would also need a micro interaction to tell them that the signup worked or failed.

I couldn't add the payment page. I also decided to skip the profile page since users would mainly need the ability to cancel their participation, IF the event allowed cancellations. Because of that, I continued with the secondary focus group, the hosts.
The secondary focus group is important for the basic function of the website. I chose to make the simulated profile the host so I could set up CRUD for this. It also solves the GDPR problem with others being able to see the private information of those who signed up.

Once an event has been made then it appears on all pages featuring events and they get added to the table in supabase as well.

solution.title: Reflections
solution.description:
My solution makes the website more usable and the code easier to navigate, but there are parts that could be improved.
If I were to go back I would take my code to a different developer to simulate a handover. Another thing I would do would be updating the design. The light green clashes with the background which is irritating for the eyes, the font used for the event titles look odd due to there being too much spacing, and the content itself is bare minimum. I would also add a proper signup page for the events and just take time to fix the userflow. In the end I did what I deemed most important for the case itself and that I had time for.

I believe that if the site was properly redesigned it could be useful for a lot of young adults who might have just moved to a bigger city. According to statistics, young adults are the most likely to be moving around and since moving means starting over, a website like this could indeed help these young adults become more integrated into the local community. This will especially benefit and be used by young adults who have trouble finding reasons to go out and for hosts to reach their target audience effectively.

title: Vuuh
shortIntro: Improving the user experience for a Shopify extension.
about:
We worked with Vuuh, a Shopify extension. They gave us their prototype and wanted to make the app more user-friendly for those who aren't native.

We were to use Heuristic Evaluation and Cognitive Walkthrough to update the user side of the site, which is what the user sees when using the extension.

For the solution, I will be focusing on explaining the parts I made due to this being a group assignment.

solution.title: Initial review
solution.description:
Doing the initial review through the eyes of new users was easy since none of us had used Shopify or Vuuh before. The second we opened the prototype we had no idea what anything was. Even the Shopify integration, which should have been easy, confused us.

We had a lot of material for our finding cards but narrowed it down to four focus points.

We deep dived into various flows to identify Heuristic issues and how to fix them. We also created a user to make tasks for. All of that can be found in the linked research file

solution.title: The optimization
solution.description:
For the optimization, we decided to focus on:
  • Onboarding tutorial
  • A wizard/task overview
  • Banners
  • Simplification of the Shopify connection process


What I oversaw was the onboarding tutorial and the process simplification.

The tutorial was made with a simple design that can be reused for each new part the user enters, but we focused on the first tutorial. Quick note, while I did make the design, the videos were made by another groupmember.

Once the tutorial is finished, the integration begins. I redesigned the process by cutting out the output page and simplifying the modal.

Once shopify has been connected, the dashboard updates too.

The prototype made for this doesn't go further other than allowing the user to enter some of the other pages.

Another thing I did was simplifying the modal for the integration process.

solution.title: Reflections
solution.description:
We managed to simplify the entire process quite a bit, but there are still parts that I think could have been optimized as well. For an example, I would like to add the little explanation on the side of the modal that the original had which explains what connecting to Shopify could do for the user's webshop. Another thing I would do would be to make more tutorials to appear for first time users when they enter a new page. The other pages like brands and output could probably also benefit from a bit more attention but overall, I think we managed to help clean up Vuuh's initial flow.

I believe with a bit more work, Vuuh could be very beneficial for Shopify users, especially those who also have a physical retail store and need some help getting properly set up with their webshop. The easier Vuuh is to use, the more likely users are to adopt it and benefit from its features.

title: LA RŌUGE
shortIntro: Creating a sub-brand focused on re-commerce.
about:
We had the opportunity to work with LA RŌUGE, a Danish fashion brand. For this case, we were asked to create and design the concept for a sub-brand that focuses on re-commerce, meaning thrifting of their own clothes. It was important that the subbrand had its own style and voice while maintaining a clear connection to LA RŌUGE. They were also aiming for potentially bringing in a new demographic with their subbrand.

For the solution, I will be focusing on explaining the parts I made due to this being a group assignment.

solution.title: Initial review
solution.description:
We began browsing LA RŌUGE, their website, and their SoMe accounts to help create our starting point.

With the style of LA RŌUGE locked down and a clearer understanding of their target group, we then moved onto the new demographic LA RŌUGE hoped to attract. LA RŌUGE itself attracts older women so they were hoping to branch out to a younger crowd. Luckily, thrifting is quite popular with younger women. We then went right ahead and made a moodboard as well as two personas (Ai Pictures) for our subbrand.

solution.title: The optimization
solution.description:
We split up so each task had one student assigned to it, with a few exceptions.

Personally, I focused on these tasks:
  • Creating wireframes
  • Create the logo
  • Creating a signature style
  • Creating the landing page
  • Creating the information page
  • Creating the return flow


I also helped with Tone of Voice and I had help with the signature style. I started with the logo which ended up having several iterations.

The name ended up being LA RŌUGE Héritage since we wanted a close connection to LA RŌUGE and Héritage means something passed down from an older generation.

With the logo done it was onto the wireframes which were made to fit a phone screen due to most young people, and LA RŌUGE customers, using phones when they shop online.

One thing we immediately agreed on was to use English as the main language due to a lot of young women in the bigger cities speaking various different languages and it's often those in the bigger cities who buy designer clothes.

After the wireframes were completed, the actual style came into play. We decided on an almost rebel-like design with lots of colors and heavy use of a stroke that made it look like the icons and buttons had been drawn up with lipstick. We went with it because we wanted to embrace the imperfect and lean into the inspiration Lassen has drawn from the Red Sock group. We also wanted to mix the elegant style of LA RŌUGE with the laid-back style of young women of today.

Instead of using professionally set up pictures of clothes on models, we wanted to use people's own pictures of them wearing the clothes they're returning. This was optional in the return process. We also added a simple way for the user to find the items they want to return, making it easy for the team behind Heritage to sort and upload them. Once you've put in your information, your former orders are displayed and you can find the exact order you're looking for.

The system was made to be simple and easy to understand since young people just want to get from A to B quickly.
But what happens if the user doesnøt want their picture on the website.
Instead of having a big team, we imagined the SoMe team consisting of a few young women who would wear the clothes and take similar pictures as resellers. We wanted to make the brand feel less staged due to the controversy around edited pictures online. The first picture on the landing page is supposed to simulate one of these girls (AI picture).

solution.title: Reflections
solution.description:
While we managed to fulfill LA RŌUGE's recommerce mission, there are a lot of areas we could continue to work on with this subbrand. We definitely want to play a bit more with the design of the buttons and whatnot to make them fit this lipstick graffiti theme we have going on. Another thing we wanted was to add the ability to browse the orders of the original buyer in case the person returning it is not the one who bought the clothes first. Obviously, this would require finding a solution that is highly secure so no one can just put in an email and find information on someone else. The last big thing that I wanted us to have done was to make a return process on the LA RŌUGE site which is targeted towards the older women. While I think our process is quick and easy, we have to keep in mind that some of these older women might not be native users like most young women are likely to be.

That said, I do believe we've managed to create an interesting subbrand that challenges the culture of perfection and could be interesting for young fashionistas to explore, especially if their moms already shop on LA RŌUGE. This would end up benefitting young women on a budget and older women who wants to buy more on LA RŌUGE without sacrificing closet space. It would also put LA RŌUGE on the radar of a younger demographic and expand their business.
